- When sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast peak by 5–10% if followed by a spike.
- If sentiment is bearish (≤0.33) and price is trending down, model often underestimates the drop; adjust downward by 3–7% to match true decline.
- Model frequently overreacts to short-term sentiment shifts — especially after 1–2 bullish sentiment spikes — leading to overshoot; apply smoothing filter or lag 1 correction.
- Mean reversion is evident in 30-day forecasts: if model shows strong upward trend after 2–3 consecutive high sentiment days, reduce slope by 15–20% to avoid overbought bias.
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.33–0.67), model often fails to capture true volatility; use sentiment-weighted average of recent 7-day mean to anchor forecast.
- For horizon > 14 days, model tends to underestimate true price movement — especially in high-sentiment periods — apply 2–5% upward bias for long-term forecasts.
- If sentiment history shows repeated “bullish → bearish” transitions, model often misjudges reversal points; delay forecast correction by 1–2 days to allow sentiment to settle.
